html:
The Aché are a hunting and gathering people of the forests of eastern Paraguay. The map shows them in 1492. Their language belongs to the Tupí Guaraní branch of the Tupian family, like that of their farming neighbours the Mbyá Guaraní, who called them Guayakí.

For centuries small Aché bands moved through the forest, living on game, palm starch, honey and insect larvae. They kept apart from colonists and from Guaraní farmers, who often raided them for captives.

In the 1960s and 1970s, as ranchers and settlers cleared their forest, the Aché were hunted down and forced onto reservations. Many died from violence and disease, and children were taken and sold. In the 1970s observers abroad accused the government of Alfredo Stroessner of genocide. A few thousand Aché live today in settled communities in Paraguay.
